guides.title: Severe bleeding
guides.summary: Heavy blood loss can kill quickly. The priority is to call for help and keep firm pressure on the wound.
guides.emergency: Call local emergency help immediately if blood is flowing heavily, spurting, rapidly soaking material, not stopping with pressure, or if the person becomes pale, confused or unresponsive.
steps: Check that the area is safe. Wear gloves if available or avoid direct contact with blood.
Expose the wound and immediately apply firm, continuous direct pressure with a dressing or clean non-fluffy cloth.
If an object is embedded, do not remove it. Press firmly on either side, never directly on the object.
Ask someone to call emergency help. If alone, use the phone speaker without stopping pressure.
Maintain pressure and do not repeatedly lift the first cloth to check. If soaked, add clean material and follow emergency instructions.
Help the person lie down if possible, keep them warm, and continuously watch their response and breathing until help arrives.
avoid: Do not remove an embedded object or probe the wound.
Do not improvise a tourniquet unless trained or directly instructed by an emergency professional.
Do not give food or drink to a seriously injured person.

guides.title: Thermal burn
guides.summary: Rapid cooling limits injury. A large or deep burn, or one affecting the face, airway, hands, genitals or a young child needs urgent help.
guides.emergency: Seek urgent medical help for any severe, large or deep burn, breathing difficulty, electrical or chemical burn, or signs of shock.
steps: Move the person away from the heat source only when it is safe to do so.
Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Do not cool the whole body.
While cooling, gently remove nearby jewellery and clothing before swelling starts, but leave anything stuck to the skin.
After cooling, cover loosely with a dry sterile dressing, clean non-fluffy cloth, or clean plastic film laid over the burn without wrapping tightly.
Keep the rest of the body warm, especially for babies, children and older people, and monitor breathing and response.
Get medical advice even if pain improves when the burn is large or affects a high-risk area.
avoid: Do not use ice, iced water, cream, oil, butter, toothpaste or powder.
Do not burst blisters or touch the burn.
Do not pull off stuck clothing or material and do not wrap a covering tightly.

guides.title: Unresponsive but breathing
guides.summary: An unresponsive person may lose protection of their airway. Check breathing and continue monitoring it.
guides.emergency: Call local emergency help. If the person is not breathing normally or is only gasping irregularly, start resuscitation according to your training or dispatcher instructions.
steps: Check that the place is safe, speak loudly to the person and gently stimulate their shoulders to look for a response.
Open the airway by gently tilting the head and lifting the chin, unless trauma guidance tells you otherwise.
For no more than 10 seconds, watch for chest movement and listen or feel for normal breathing.
If unresponsive but breathing normally, and no injury prevents movement, roll the person onto their side in the recovery position.
Keep the head slightly tilted back, mouth pointing down, and call or send someone for emergency help.
Stay and check breathing often. If it becomes abnormal, roll them onto their back and begin guided resuscitation.
avoid: Never leave an unresponsive person alone.
Do not give anything to eat or drink.
Do not treat irregular gasps as normal breathing.

guides.title: After an unexpected birth
guides.summary: This guide starts after the baby has been born. It does not replace a skilled birth attendant or describe advanced obstetric procedures.
guides.emergency: Get skilled help immediately for both mother and baby. Heavy bleeding, an unresponsive mother, or a baby who is not breathing normally, remains blue, very floppy or cold are absolute emergencies.
steps: Call skilled medical help and follow their instructions. Wash your hands if possible and prepare clean, dry, warm cloths.
As soon as the baby is born, dry them thoroughly with a clean dry cloth while checking breathing. Remove the wet cloth.
If breathing, place the baby skin-to-skin on the mother’s chest, cover them both and cover the baby’s head to retain warmth.
If the baby is not breathing or is gasping, call for help, gently rub the back two or three times and immediately follow professional resuscitation instructions.
Do not pull the cord or placenta. Keep the cord clean and dry and put no substance on it.
If mother and baby are stable, support early breastfeeding and arrange professional assessment as soon as possible.
avoid: Do not hang or shake the baby and do not routinely suction the mouth or nose.
Do not bathe the baby or leave them wet or uncovered.
Do not pull or cut the cord without training, clean equipment or professional instruction.
